Overstatement: no source says the proponents expect plug-ins 'first'. The FAQ says agents 'can be as simple as browser plugins (and Web server plugins on the other side)'. Minor wording: the FAQ says 'browser headers', not 'HTTP headers'. DNT and GPC are HTTP request headers, so the gloss is defensible, but the corrected text follows the source.

'AI agents later' is supported only loosely, by the FAQ's 'AI will likely be more involved as development of MyTerms products and services proceed and evolve'. The published abstract, unlike the 2017 PAR, already names 'AI agents' among the covered services. The rewritten summary reflects this.

fieldFixes.summary: Agents for both parties may use any protocol that serves the purpose; the standard does not specify the technology. The proponents' early sketches centre on browser and web-server plug-ins (the FAQ suggests signalling through browser headers on the model of Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control), and they expect AI to play a larger part as products develop; MyData Global (August 2026) lists apps, digital wallets and agentic AI among possible agents and says personal agents have been built for release in Q4 2026.

issues: All three quotes --check FOUND on 2026-09-23. The DPV page is 'Extension for IEEE P7012 (P7012) version 2.1, Draft Community Group Report 16 March 2025' (editor H. J. Pandit; authors Esteves, Pandit, Henderson), and it cites IEEE-P7012, the draft.

Misleading framing: the summary presents the single counter-offer as a DPV-only reading that 'differs from the published abstract'. In fact the MyTerms proponents describe the same limited back-and-forth after publication. MyData Global, part of the launch team, wrote on 20 Jan 2026 that the standard 'enables organisations to accept these proposals, or to propose an alternative from the same list'. Doc Searls, the WG chair, wrote on 7 Jan 2026 that the standard 'is not about negotiation. It’s about choice'. He added that a person may offer 'a first and second choice of agreement, but no more than that', and his MAR sketch lists an 'accept / refuse / counter-offer choice'. The DPV text also was not superseded: v2.2 (Draft CG Report, 01 August 2025) repeats 'negotiations are limited to a single counter-offer'.

The corrected summary keeps the scope rule from the abstract. It says the permitted moves are a choice among roster agreements, not bargaining over their terms, and names v2.2 alongside the March 2025 draft.

fieldFixes.summary: The person points to a preferred agreement (or a set) and the organisation accepts one; party-to-party negotiation over the terms of any agreement is out of scope. If the organisation says no, the person's agent can record the refusal. What the proponents describe is choice among roster agreements, not bargaining: Doc Searls (January 2026) says a person may offer 'a first and second choice of agreement, but no more than that'; MyData Global says organisations may accept or propose an alternative from the same list; and the W3C DPV community group's P7012 extension (v2.1, March 2025, repeated in v2.2, August 2025), written against a draft, allows the organisation's agent a single counter-offer drawn from the registry. The published abstract itself does not mention counter-offers.

issues: All three quotes --check FOUND on 2026-09-23. The archived Customer Commons page came from the helper cache because web.archive.org reset connections during this check.

Tense and support: the only source for 'launched' is the Standard page, which is still in the future tense ('MyTerms will launch with 5 ... We will then update'; the page was last modified 2026-02-14). That the launch actually happened is shown by myterms.info/news: 'MyTerms Kicked Off to large online and in-person crowd at Imperial College London' and 'Re-watch our Launch on YouTube from January 28, 2026'. MyData Global's 20 Jan 2026 post gave the date as Wednesday 28 January 2026 (Data Privacy Day), 'in London and online', with SD-BASE plus 'four further agreements available at launch'. Those sources are added. The six-month feedback window is still only a stated plan. As of 2026-09-23 no source found announces the updated agreements or the 'full market launch'.

'A 2025 Customer Commons page' overstates what we know about the page's date. The Wayback availability API returns 2025-10-06 as the closest snapshot even for 2023 and 2024 timestamps, so no earlier capture exists. The page carries old '0.9' agreements (NoStalking, P2B1) in 'demo phase', so its text may predate 2025. Reworded to 'a Customer Commons page archived in October 2025'.
The five agreements named on the Standard page are SD-BASE, SD-BASE-DP, PDC-AI, PDC-GOOD and PDC-INTENT. The FAQ says '5 agreements when we launch MyTerms, and 8 more in the pipeline' (FOUND).

fieldFixes.summary: MyTerms said it would launch with five standardised agreements (SD-BASE, SD-BASE-DP, PDC-AI, PDC-GOOD and PDC-INTENT) and run in that mode for up to six months to gather market feedback before updating them for a full market launch. The public launch took place on 28 January 2026 at Imperial College London and online. The FAQ says eight more agreements are in the pipeline; a Customer Commons page archived in October 2025 had said eleven more.

issues: Both quotes re-fetched on 2026-09-23 and --check FOUND on https://www.w3.org/TR/P3P/. The page header reads 'W3C Recommendation 16 April 2002 obsoleted 30 August 2018' (This Version: TR/2018/OBSL-P3P-20180830/). That matches year 2002, yearEnd 2018 and the fate text.

The fate's 'limited deployment' was not in any quoted text, although the same status section says it. That sentence is added as a source. The same section notes that fewer than 6% of the top 10,000 sites supported P3P in 2018, that no current user agents implemented it, and that IE's use of compact policies as a cookie gate led sites to copy generic policies.

The note ('users' agents could only accept or reject them') is a fair simplification of the W3C description. User agents would 'accept some practices automatically ... or ... prompt the user for further instruction'.
